text: A variable is just a name pointing at a value in memory. In data engineering, variables usually represent fields from a real record — not abstract placeholders. This lesson covers naming values, the core types, and the type mix-up that's probably the single most common bug new data engineers hit.

Order ID, customer name, quantity, unit price — each one gets a name, an equals sign, and a value. Python figures out the type from what you assign, so you never declare int order_id the way some other languages require. That convenience is also the risk: nothing stops you from later reassigning order_id to a string by mistake.

Five core types: int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, bool for True or False, and None, which deserves its own callout — it's not zero, not an empty string, and not False. It's Python's explicit way of saying a field genuinely has no value. type of lets you confirm exactly what Python decided.

Arithmetic operators like star and plus compute a new value. Comparison operators — double equals, not equals, less than, greater than — always hand back a bool. And logical operators, and, or, not, combine bool values together, which is exactly the kind of check you'll write constantly when validating incoming data starting in Chapter 6.

Here's the real bug: a field read from a file often arrives as a string even when it looks like a number. Multiply that string by a float and Python raises a TypeError — it won't silently guess what you meant. The fix is converting explicitly with int, a pattern you'll use constantly once you start reading real text files in Chapter 3.

You now know the five core types, how operators work, and why string-versus-number mix-ups bite real pipelines. Next lesson: strings and string formatting — cleaning up messy text and building readable output with f-strings, the tools you'll reach for in almost every script from here on.
